method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
steps: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size (a ratio, no unit).
Rearrange: actual = image ÷ magnification; image = actual × magnification.
Put both lengths in the SAME unit before dividing.
1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 µm = 1000 nm. To smaller units multiply by 1000; to larger units divide.
method_card.content:
Magnification tells you how many times bigger an image is than the real object. It is a ratio, so it has no unit.

The three forms: magnification = image ÷ actual; actual = image ÷ magnification; image = actual × magnification.

The biggest mark-killer is mixed units. Always convert so the image size and actual size share one unit before you divide. Check whether your board wants the answer in mm, µm or nm.

Conversions: 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 µm = 1000 nm. Moving to a smaller unit multiplies by 1000; moving to a larger unit divides by 1000.

exam_context.frequency: Medium to high: magnification questions appear regularly

gold.display: A chloroplast has an actual diameter of 5 µm. An electron microscope image of it is 40 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
gold.question: A chloroplast has an actual diameter of 5 µm. An electron microscope image of it is 40 mm wide. Calculate the magnification.
gold.equation_hint: Convert µm to mm, then magnification = image ÷ actual.
gold.hint: The lengths are in different units, so convert first, then divide image by actual.

misconceptions.message: The image is in mm and the cell in µm. Convert 5 µm to 0.005 mm, then 40 ÷ 0.005 = 8000. Dividing 40 by 5 ignores the unit mismatch.
Magnification = image ÷ actual = 40 ÷ 0.005 = 8000, not actual ÷ image.

guided_steps.say: The image is in mm and the cell in µm, so convert first, then magnification = image ÷ actual size.

guided_steps.done: Back to 40 mm, so the magnification is ×8000.

gold.display: A virus is 150 nm in diameter. Calculate this diameter in µm.
gold.equation_hint: Divide by 1,000 to go from nm to µm
gold.hint: nm to µm moves to larger units, so divide by 1000.

misconceptions.message: nm to µm makes the number smaller, so divide by 1000: 150 ÷ 1000 = 0.15 µm.

guided_steps.say: Going from nm to µm moves to larger units, so the number gets smaller. The rule: 1000 nm = 1 µm.

guided_steps.pre: How many nm are in 1 µm?

guided_steps.hint: 150 ÷ 1000 moves the decimal three places left.

guided_steps.done: Back to 150 nm, so 150 nm = 0.15 µm.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.007 mm, which is 7 µm, so the drawing is 10.5 mm wide.

opener.display:
A ladybird is 5 mm long in real life.
In a photo it measures 60 mm across.

steps.pre: No formula yet, just common sense. How many times bigger does the photo make the ladybird look?
steps.say: The photo makes the ladybird look bigger. Compare the two lengths.

steps.pre: A beetle is really 8 mm long. A photo magnifies it 10 times. How long is it in the photo, in mm?
steps.say: That 'how many times bigger' number is the magnification. You just did image size ÷ actual size = 60 ÷ 5.

So magnification = image size ÷ actual size, a pure ratio with no unit. The one rule that catches people: both lengths must be in the SAME unit before you divide. Real cells are often measured in µm while the image is in mm, so converting units first is the whole skill.
